title: Processor Fundamentals + Parameter Passing
instructions: Answer all questions. Section A covers processor fundamentals, Section B covers parameter passing. Part labels match the original paper. Calculators are not permitted.

questions.text: **Question 1** — Which statement describes the **stored-program concept** in the von Neumann model?

options.text: Program instructions and data are both stored in memory.
Program instructions are stored in the control unit and data in the ALU.
Programs are stored on permanent ROM and data in RAM.
Instructions are stored in registers and data on the hard disk.

questions.explanation:
**A.** Both instructions *and* data live in the same memory — that is the defining feature of von Neumann. It is why a program can be treated as data (loaded, moved, even modified).

You picked this and the portal's feedback said "not the accepted answer" — that feedback is wrong; your answer is correct. The distractor it probably wanted was B (instructions in the control unit), which confuses *execution* with *storage*: the CU decodes the instruction in the CIR, it does not store the program.

questions.text: **Question 2** — Which component is responsible for **arithmetic and logical operations**?
questions.explanation:
**B.** The ALU performs arithmetic (add, subtract, multiply) and logic (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons, shifts).

The CU only *directs* operations: it decodes the instruction and sends control signals telling the ALU what to do. Again the portal's "not accepted" feedback is wrong for this answer.

questions.text: **Question 3** — Which register stores the address of the **next instruction** to be fetched?
questions.explanation:
**C.** The PC holds the address of the next instruction; it is incremented during the fetch stage.

MAR holds the address currently *being* accessed (they are equal for one moment during fetch — that is Q14(a)(i): `MAR ← [PC]`). CIR holds the instruction itself, not its address.

questions.text: **Question 4** — Which **system bus** is **unidirectional**?
questions.explanation:
**C — the address bus.** The CPU puts an address onto it and memory responds; nothing travels back along it, so it is unidirectional.

The data bus is **bidirectional** (data is both read and written). The control bus is often described as bidirectional too, because signals like *interrupt request* travel from devices to the CPU while *read/write* travel from the CPU outward — individual lines are one-way, but the bus as a whole carries both directions.

questions.text: **Question 5** — Which change **directly increases the number of memory locations** that can be addressed?

options.text: Increasing the width of the data bus
Increasing the width of the address bus
Increasing the size of the MDR

questions.explanation:
**B.** Addressable locations = 2^(address bus width). A 24-bit address bus gives 2^24 = 16 777 216 locations.

Data bus width controls how many bits move *per transfer*, not how many locations exist. Clock speed only affects how fast you reach them.

questions.text: **Question 6** — The register that stores the instruction currently being **decoded and executed** is the:
questions.explanation: **B — CIR (Current Instruction Register).** The instruction is copied from the MDR into the CIR at the end of the fetch stage, then the CU decodes it from there.

questions.text: **Question 7** — The system bus that carries **read/write and timing signals** is the:
questions.explanation: **C — Control bus.** It carries the CU's command and timing signals: read/write, clock pulses, interrupt requests and acknowledgements.

questions.text: **Question 8** — The register used to hold data **read from memory or about to be written** to memory is the:
questions.explanation:
**C — MDR (Memory Data Register)** — sometimes called the MBR (Memory Buffer Register). It is the bidirectional buffer between the CPU and memory, and it sits directly on the data bus.

Quick way to keep MAR and MDR apart: **MAR = address, MDR = data**.

questions.text: **Question 9** — The interface that transmits **both high-quality video and audio** to a display is:
questions.explanation:
**C — HDMI.** It carries digital video *and* audio on one cable.

VGA is analogue video only, with no audio — that is the distinction examiners test. USB and Ethernet are general data interfaces, not display standards.

questions.text: **Question 10 (a)** — State the purpose of the **Memory Address Register (MAR)**.

answer.text: Holds the address of the memory location currently being read from or written to

questions.explanation:
The MAR holds the **address** of the location currently being accessed — for either a data item or an instruction.

One-line answers are fine here: 1 mark for "address of the location being accessed". Do not write "stores data" — that is the MDR.

questions.text: **Question 10 (b)** — State the purpose of the **Program Counter (PC)**.

answer.text: Holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched

questions.explanation:
The PC holds the **address of the next instruction** to be fetched from memory, and is incremented as part of the fetch stage.

"Next" is the mark-earning word. Saying "the current instruction" loses the mark — that is the CIR.

questions.text: **Question 10 (c)** — State the purpose of the **Status Register (SR)**.

answer.text: Stores flags / status bits that record the result of arithmetic or logical operations (e.g. overflow, zero, negative, carry)

questions.explanation:
The SR (also called the flag register) holds **condition flags** set by the ALU — carry, overflow, zero, sign — which later conditional instructions (e.g. a branch) test.

Mentioning a named flag (overflow/zero/carry) is what separates a full-mark answer from a vague one.

questions.text: **Question 11 (a)** — Explain how **increasing the processor clock speed** improves performance.

answer.text: More clock cycles per second, so more fetch-decode-execute cycles complete each second

questions.explanation:
Clock speed is cycles per second. Each F-E cycle needs a fixed number of cycles, so a higher clock rate → more instructions completed per second.

The trap is writing "the CPU works faster" — that restates the question. Name the **F-E cycle** and the mark is secure.

questions.text: **Question 11 (b)** — Explain how **increasing cache memory capacity** improves performance.

answer.text: Cache is faster than main memory (RAM), so more frequently used data/instructions can be held there, reducing waiting for slower main memory

questions.explanation:
Cache is built from SRAM and sits close to (often on) the CPU, so it is much faster than RAM. A **larger** cache holds **more** frequently used instructions and data, so proportionally more accesses hit the cache instead of waiting on main memory.

Note the portal's own feedback: your answer matched the rubric but didn't explicitly say *larger cache holds more data* — include that phrase to be safe.

questions.text: **Question 11 (c)** — Explain how **increasing the number of processor cores** improves performance.

answer.text: Multiple instruction streams can be processed simultaneously (in parallel), increasing overall throughput

questions.explanation:
Each core can execute its own instruction stream, so independent tasks/threads run **in parallel** rather than time-sliced, raising throughput.

Don't claim that a single program automatically runs N times faster — only parallelisable work benefits.

questions.text: **Question 12 (a)** — State what is meant by a **port** in a computer system.

answer.text: A connection/interface point that allows a peripheral device to be attached and to communicate/transfer data with the computer

questions.explanation:
A port is the **interface/socket** where a peripheral connects — the physical and logical point where data enters or leaves the system.

Alternative mark point: a numbered logical channel used to route data to a specific process (e.g. port 80) — also acceptable if the question is about networking.

questions.text: **Question 12 (b)** — Explain **two features of USB** that make it suitable for connecting peripheral devices.

answer.text: Plug-and-play: the device is detected automatically and the driver is loaded without a reboot / no configuration needed
It can supply power to the device, so a separate power supply is not needed

questions.explanation:
Any **two distinct, explained** features. Reliable pairs to memorise:

| Feature | Why it makes USB suitable |
|---|---|
| Plug-and-play / hot-swappable | OS detects the device and loads the driver automatically, no reboot |
| Provides power | Many devices need no separate power supply |
| Universal standard | One connector type works across many device types and manufacturers |
| Serial, asynchronous transfer | Fewer wires, cheap cable, reliable over short distance |
| Backwards compatible | Versions interoperate (USB 2.0 device in a 3.0 port) |

**Two features, each explained** — a bare list earns at most half. Your paper answer used plug-and-play + asynchronous serial, which is why it got 2/2.

questions.text: **Question 13 (a)** — State the register that **initially** contains the address of the next instruction.

answer.text: Program Counter (PC)

questions.explanation: **Program Counter.** "Initially" is the hint: the PC holds it before the fetch stage copies it to the MAR.

questions.text: **Question 13 (b)** — Describe how the instruction is transferred from memory into the **Current Instruction Register (CIR)** during the fetch stage.

answer.text: The address in the PC is copied to the MAR
The instruction at that address is fetched from memory into the MDR (data travels on the data bus)
The instruction is then copied from the MDR into the CIR

questions.explanation:
Three stages, in order:

1. `MAR ← [PC]` — the PC's address goes to the MAR, and is placed on the address bus.
2. `MDR ← [[MAR]]` — memory returns the instruction on the data bus into the MDR.
3. `CIR ← [MDR]` — the instruction is copied into the CIR, ready to be decoded.

The "one mark per stage" pattern is deliberate. Write all three even if you are unsure — partial credit is generous.

questions.text:
**Question 14 (a)** — Write the register transfer notation for each step of the fetch stage.

(i) The address of the next instruction is copied from the PC to the MAR.

(ii) The PC is incremented by 1.

(iii) The instruction stored at the memory address held in the MAR is copied into the MDR.

(iv) The instruction in the MDR is copied into the CIR.

answer.text: (i) MAR ← [PC]
(ii) PC ← [PC] + 1
(iii) MDR ← [[MAR]]
(iv) CIR ← [MDR]

questions.explanation:
The four lines, exactly:

```
MAR ← [PC]
PC  ← [PC] + 1
MDR ← [[MAR]]
CIR ← [MDR]
```

**Notation rules the examiner enforces:**
- `←` for assignment, never `=`.
- `[X]` means *contents of* X. So `[PC]` = contents of the PC = an address; `[[MAR]]` = contents of the location whose address is in MAR = the instruction itself. The **double brackets** are the bit most candidates miss.
- In (iii) the destination is the **MDR**, not the CIR — the instruction moves MDR → CIR only in step (iv).

questions.text: **Question 14 (b)** — Rewrite operations (a)(ii) and (a)(iii) on a **single line** using the correct notation to indicate that they occur **simultaneously**.

answer.text: PC ← [PC] + 1; MDR ← [[MAR]]

questions.explanation:
`PC ← [PC] + 1 ; MDR ← [[MAR]]`

A **semicolon** separates two register transfers that happen in the same clock cycle. This matters because incrementing the PC does not depend on the memory read, so the hardware performs both at once — the reason fetch takes fewer cycles than you would expect.

questions.text: **Question 15 (a)** — State **one** possible cause of an **interrupt**.

answer.text: A hardware fault or event — e.g. a printer running out of paper, a device completing an I/O transfer, a timer signal, or a software error such as division by zero

questions.explanation:
Any one valid cause. Good examples: printer out of paper, I/O transfer complete, hardware timer tick, power failure, division by zero (software interrupt).

Name a **specific** device or event; "a problem" alone is too vague for the mark.

questions.text: **Question 15 (b)** — Describe the sequence of actions taken by the processor to **handle an interrupt and resume** the original program.

answer.text: The processor finishes the current fetch-execute cycle, then checks the **interrupt register** / interrupt flags (not the status register, which holds ALU flags)
The current register contents and the return address (PC) are saved to a stack
It identifies the interrupt priority and runs the relevant Interrupt Service Routine (ISR); when finished, the saved register values are restored from the stack so the main program resumes

questions.explanation:
Three mark-worthy stages:

1. **Complete the current instruction** (never abandon it mid-execution), then check for interrupts.
2. **Save state** — push register contents and the return address onto the stack.
3. **Identify and service** — find which device interrupted (highest priority first), run its ISR, then **restore** the registers from the stack and continue.

The words that earn marks: *current instruction completed*, *stack*, *ISR*, *priority*, *restore*. An answer that jumps straight to "runs the ISR" loses the state-saving mark.

**Precision matters here:** the interrupt is detected by checking the **interrupt register** at the end of the cycle — the *status register* holds ALU flags (carry, overflow, zero, sign) and is a different thing. Writing "status register" in this answer is the single most common way to lose the first mark.

questions.text: **Question 16 (a)** — State the values output for **A** and **B**.
questions.explanation:
**A = 5, B = 10.**

This is the classic BYVAL/BYREF contrast: the BYVAL parameter changes only its local copy (so the original stays 5), while the BYREF parameter is changed in place (so the original becomes 10).

The portal marked your 5/10 as "0/0 response(s) correct" — that is a bug in its marking, not an error in your answer.

questions.text: **Question 16 (b)** — Explain the difference between passing a parameter **BYVAL** and **BYREF**.

answer.text: BYVAL passes a copy of the value, so changes inside the procedure do not affect the original variable
BYREF passes the address/reference of the original variable, so changes inside the procedure directly update the original

questions.explanation:
Two halves, and you need both:

- **BYVAL** — a *copy* of the value is passed. The subroutine works on its own local copy; the caller's variable is protected from change.
- **BYREF** — the *address* is passed. The subroutine works on the original storage, so changes are visible to the caller.

Say what happens **to the original**, not just the mechanism. "BYREF passes the address" alone gets half a mark; add "so the original is modified".

questions.text: **Question 16 (c)** — A student wants `ChangeValue` to modify the **original** value of `A`. State the change required to the procedure declaration and explain why this change works.

answer.text: Change `BYVAL` to `BYREF` in the parameter header, e.g. `PROCEDURE ChangeValue(BYREF Num : INTEGER)`
Passing by reference gives the procedure the actual memory address of A, so any change to Num inside the procedure updates the original variable rather than a copy

questions.explanation:
The change: **`BYVAL` → `BYREF`** in the parameter header.

```
PROCEDURE ChangeValue(BYREF Num : INTEGER)
```

Why it works: BYREF passes the *address* of `A`, so `Num` and `A` refer to the same storage location. Assigning to `Num` therefore writes straight through to `A`.

The explanation must mention **the original variable being updated directly** (or "the address is passed") — that is the second mark.

questions.text:
**Question 17 (a)** — Write a procedure named `DisplayBonus` that:

• accepts an **INTEGER** parameter named `Score`
• adds **5** to `Score` and outputs the updated score
• must **not** change the original value of the variable passed to the procedure

answer.text: Correct header using **BYVAL**, typed: `PROCEDURE DisplayBonus(BYVAL Score : INTEGER)`
`Score ← Score + 5`
`OUTPUT Score` and a matching `ENDPROCEDURE`

questions.explanation:
```
PROCEDURE DisplayBonus(BYVAL Score : INTEGER)
    Score ← Score + 5
    OUTPUT Score
ENDPROCEDURE
```

"Must not change the original" is the instruction to use **BYVAL** — that single keyword is worth a mark on its own. Then the update, the output, and the `ENDPROCEDURE`.

Notice how many marks come from structure rather than logic: header (1), update (1), output + close (1).

questions.text:
**Question 17 (b)** — Write a procedure named `ApplyBonus` that:

• accepts an **INTEGER** parameter named `Score`
• adds **10** to `Score` and must **permanently update** the original variable passed to the procedure
• does **not** output a value

answer.text: Correct header using **BYREF**, typed: `PROCEDURE ApplyBonus(BYREF Score : INTEGER)`
`Score ← Score + 10`
Correct `ENDPROCEDURE` with **no** `OUTPUT` statement

questions.explanation:
```
PROCEDURE ApplyBonus(BYREF Score : INTEGER)
    Score ← Score + 10
ENDPROCEDURE
```

"Permanently update the original" → **BYREF**. "Does not output" → no `OUTPUT` at all; adding one loses that mark.

Pair 17(a) and 17(b) in your head: **BYVAL = display a calculated copy, BYREF = change the real thing.**

questions.text:
**Question 17 (c)** — Write a main program that:

• declares an INTEGER variable named `StudentScore` and assigns it the value **60**
• calls `DisplayBonus`, followed by `ApplyBonus`, passing `StudentScore` to both procedures
• outputs the **final** value of `StudentScore`

> **Note on the mark scheme:** this part is worth 2 marks on the paper but has 3 criteria (declaration + value, the two calls in order, the final output). The scorer caps your ticks at 2 — tick the two you are most confident about.

answer.text: `DECLARE StudentScore : INTEGER` and `StudentScore ← 60`
`CALL DisplayBonus(StudentScore)` then `CALL ApplyBonus(StudentScore)`, in that order
`OUTPUT StudentScore` at the end

questions.explanation:
```
DECLARE StudentScore : INTEGER
StudentScore ← 60

CALL DisplayBonus(StudentScore)
CALL ApplyBonus(StudentScore)

OUTPUT StudentScore
```

**Trace it through** — this is the whole point of the question:

| Step | StudentScore | Output |
|---|---|---|
| `StudentScore ← 60` | 60 | — |
| `DisplayBonus` (BYVAL) | **60** (unchanged — it edited a copy) | prints 65 |
| `ApplyBonus` (BYREF) | **70** (real change: 60 + 10) | — |
| `OUTPUT StudentScore` | 70 | prints **70** |

You left this blank on the paper, which cost 2 free marks. Even without the exact arithmetic you would have earned the declaration mark and probably the calls mark.

**The biggest Paper 2 lesson in this paper:** a blank scores zero, but `DECLARE` + a value + two `CALL` lines + an `OUTPUT` earn most of the marks even when the logic is imperfect. Always write something.
